units.title: Unit 43 — Colour and light
units.source: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition); printed pages 90–91 (PDF pages 94–95).
units.bookTitle: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition)
units.category: Basic concepts · colour, light and figurative language
learningObjectives: Describe bright, pale, dark and subdued colours and how clothes coordinate.
Distinguish colour fading during use from dye running during washing.
Describe changing light, glare, twinkling, and faint or concentrated sources of light.
Interpret figurative colour and light expressions while retaining their natural prepositions.

items.section: A · Describing colours
items.example: Bright colours can make a small room feel more cheerful.
items.note: Bright means vivid and visually striking rather than pale or muted.

items.section: A · Describing colours
items.example: The office furniture was chosen in subdued colours.
items.note: Subdued describes colours that are restrained and not very bright; compare bright colours.

items.section: A · Describing colours
items.example: The old curtains had dull colours that made the room look gloomy.
items.note: Dull colours lack brightness or vividness and often seem uninteresting.

items.section: A · Describing colours
items.example: She chose bright yellow for the kitchen walls.
items.note: Bright intensifies the vividness of a colour and is not the same as pale.

items.section: A · Describing colours
items.example: The children painted the door bright green.
items.note: A vivid shade of green; different from the soft shade pale green.

items.section: A · Describing colours
items.example: He bought a pale blue shirt for the ceremony.
items.note: Pale describes a light, low-intensity shade rather than a bright one.

items.section: A · Describing colours
items.example: A pale green scarf would go nicely with that coat.
items.note: Pale green denotes a delicate, low-intensity shade and features in the unit’s matching exercise.

items.section: A · Describing colours
items.example: The bedroom walls are painted dark green.
items.note: Dark describes a deep shade; it does not necessarily mean dull or subdued.

items.section: A · Describing colours
items.example: The colour fades if you leave this fabric in direct sunlight.
items.note: Fade refers to a colour gradually becoming less strong, for example through sun exposure or washing.

items.pt: a tinta soltou; a cor manchou outras peças
items.section: A · Describing colours
items.example: The colour ran when I washed the new scarf with white towels.
items.note: When a colour runs, dye spreads into the water and may stain other clothes; ran is the past tense.

items.section: A · Describing colours
items.example: These colours go well together without looking identical.
items.note: Use go well together when two or more colours look harmonious; they need not match exactly.

items.section: A · Describing colours
items.example: The colours clash because the orange is too strong beside the purple.
items.note: Clash suggests an unpleasant visual combination, contrasting with go well together.

items.section: A · Describing colours
items.example: These shoes match the jacket perfectly.
items.note: Match means suit or correspond in colour or style; a matching item need not be identical.

items.section: A · Describing colours
items.example: Fresh flowers gave the entrance hall a touch of colour.
items.note: A touch of means a small amount that makes something more attractive or varied.

items.section: A · Describing colours
items.example: A patterned cushion can add a touch of colour to the sofa.
items.note: The pattern add a touch of colour to something names a small decorative improvement.

items.section: B · Describing light
items.example: The sky began to grow dark before the storm.
items.note: Grow dark is a descriptive way to say that daylight is gradually disappearing.

items.pt: uma vela tremula; a chama de uma vela oscila
items.section: B · Describing light
items.example: A candle flickers whenever the door opens.
items.note: Flicker means burn or shine unsteadily, usually because the flame is affected by air movement.

items.section: B · Describing light
items.example: A beam of light crossed the dusty attic.
items.note: Beam denotes a directed, concentrated strip of light, often from a torch or headlight.

items.pt: um feixe de luz intenso; um facho de luz potente
items.section: B · Describing light
items.example: A powerful beam of light came from the search helicopter.
items.note: Powerful describes the strength of a focused beam of light.

items.section: B · Describing light
items.example: A ray of sunlight reached the floor through a narrow gap.
items.note: Ray typically refers to light from the sun; beam is more common for a torch or spotlight.

items.pt: o ofuscamento causado pelo sol; a luz intensa do sol
items.section: B · Describing light
items.example: The glare of the sun made the road signs difficult to read.
items.note: Glare is unpleasantly strong light that can make seeing difficult; do not confuse it with a gentle glow.

items.section: B · Describing light
items.example: Stars twinkle above the village on clear nights.
items.note: Twinkle describes points of light seeming to flash or vary; shine is more general and steady.

items.section: B · Describing light
items.example: We spotted a pinpoint of light on the distant hillside.
items.note: A pinpoint of light is an extremely small visible spot, often seen far away.

items.section: B · Describing light
items.example: The cellar was pitch dark after the electricity failed.
items.note: Pitch dark describes complete darkness, especially of a place or night.

items.pt: um brilho fraco; uma luminosidade tênue
items.section: B · Describing light
items.example: A faint glow appeared behind the curtains.
items.note: Faint means weak or barely visible, while glow suggests soft, diffuse light.

items.section: B · Describing light
items.example: The faint glow of dawn appeared above the rooftops.
items.note: The phrase describes the gentle light visible as night gives way to morning.

items.pt: tingido de dourado; com tons dourados
items.section: B · Describing light
items.example: The clouds were tinged with gold at sunset.
items.note: Tinged with describes a small amount or trace of colour mixed into something else.

items.section: B · Describing light
items.example: It was pitch black outside the tent when we woke up.
items.note: In the exercise key, pitch black is appropriate for total darkness; it is less natural for describing hair.

items.pt: cabelo preto intenso; cabelo negro como azeviche
items.section: B · Describing light
items.example: Her jet-black hair stood out against the white coat.
items.note: Jet black describes a very deep black, naturally used for hair; contrast pitch black for darkness.

items.section: B · Describing light
items.example: A star shines steadily near the horizon in the photograph.
items.note: Shines is a general term for emitting light; twinkles suggests apparent small fluctuations.

items.pt: uma área cinzenta; uma questão sem definição clara
items.section: C · Colour and light: metaphorical collocations
items.example: The policy leaves a grey area about who approves expenses.
items.note: A grey area is a situation in which rules or distinctions are unclear; it does not mean a grey-coloured place.

items.pt: dar mais vida; tornar a vida mais interessante
items.section: C · Colour and light: metaphorical collocations
items.example: Travelling and meeting new people can add colour to life.
items.note: Figurative add colour to makes an experience livelier or more interesting.

items.pt: dar mais vida a uma história
items.section: C · Colour and light: metaphorical collocations
items.example: Small details can add colour to a story without changing its facts.
items.note: Here colour is figurative: vivid and engaging detail, not literal colour.

items.section: C · Colour and light: metaphorical collocations
items.example: The election debate included several green issues.
items.note: Green can refer to environmental protection rather than the literal colour.

items.pt: difamar alguém; manchar a reputação de alguém
items.section: C · Colour and light: metaphorical collocations
items.example: The false accusation was designed to blacken someone's name rather than reveal the truth.
items.note: Blacken someone’s name means harm their reputation, typically by saying damaging things.

items.section: C · Colour and light: metaphorical collocations
items.example: Could this email shed some light on why the meeting was cancelled?
items.note: Shed some light on means make something unclear easier to understand; retain on.

items.section: C · Colour and light: metaphorical collocations
items.example: The inspection report may throw some light on the failure.
items.note: A natural alternative to shed some light on; both take on before the subject of explanation.

items.pt: lançar uma sombra sobre; prejudicar o clima de
items.section: C · Colour and light: metaphorical collocations
items.example: The disappointing news cast a shadow over their celebrations.
items.note: Figurative cast a shadow over means make an otherwise happy event less enjoyable.

items.section: C · Colour and light: metaphorical collocations
items.example: He spent years working under the shadow of his successful father.
items.note: Figurative under the shadow of describes living with less attention or confidence because of another person.

units.title: Unit 44 — Texture
units.source: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition); printed pages 92–93 (PDF pages 96–97).
units.bookTitle: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition)
units.category: Basic concepts · surfaces, consistency and figurative texture
learningObjectives: Choose conventional adjective–noun partners for skin, hair, water, roads, bedding, food and tools.
Contrast literal textures such as smooth/rough, tender/tough, sharp/blunt and soft/firm.
Use melt, thaw, go soft/hard, soften and harden correctly.
Describe finishes, food preparation and hair appearance, and recognise figurative texture expressions.

items.section: A · Adjectives and their opposites for describing textures
items.example: This conditioner is suitable for dry hair.
items.note: Dry hair lacks moisture; the contrasting texture in the table is greasy hair.

items.section: A · Adjectives and their opposites for describing textures
items.example: He uses a gentle shampoo because he has greasy hair.
items.note: Greasy describes excessive oil in hair; dry hair is its contrast in the unit.

items.section: A · Adjectives and their opposites for describing textures
items.example: Cold weather often makes dry skin feel uncomfortable.
items.note: Dry skin needs moisture; oily skin is a contrasting common skin type.

items.section: A · Adjectives and their opposites for describing textures
items.example: She chooses lightweight moisturiser for oily skin.
items.note: Oily describes skin that produces a lot of oil; greasy skin is also possible.

items.section: A · Adjectives and their opposites for describing textures
items.example: A heavy cream can sometimes leave greasy skin feeling uncomfortable.
items.note: The answer key also accepts greasy skin as an alternative to oily skin.

items.section: A · Adjectives and their opposites for describing textures
items.example: The lotion left her hands with smooth skin.
items.note: Smooth skin has an even surface, contrasting with rough skin.

items.section: A · Adjectives and their opposites for describing textures
items.example: The cold wind left him with rough skin around his knuckles.
items.note: Rough skin feels uneven or coarse to the touch.

items.section: A · Adjectives and their opposites for describing textures
items.example: The table has a smooth surface that is easy to clean.
items.note: A smooth surface has few irregularities; rough surface means uneven to the touch.

items.section: A · Adjectives and their opposites for describing textures
items.example: The old wall has a rough surface under the paint.
items.note: Rough is the natural contrast with smooth when discussing how a surface feels.

items.pt: pele do rosto lisa; tez uniforme
items.section: A · Adjectives and their opposites for describing textures
items.example: She has a smooth complexion despite the cold weather.
items.note: Complexion refers to the appearance and condition of facial skin.

items.pt: tez áspera; pele do rosto áspera
items.section: A · Adjectives and their opposites for describing textures
items.example: The dry climate had left him with a rough complexion.
items.note: Here complexion is the facial skin’s condition; smooth complexion is the contrast.

items.section: A · Adjectives and their opposites for describing textures
items.example: The crew were relieved to find a smooth sea at sunrise.
items.note: Smooth sea describes a calm, nearly flat surface; choppy or rough sea is its opposite.

items.section: A · Adjectives and their opposites for describing textures
items.example: The small boat struggled in the choppy sea.
items.note: Choppy describes short, irregular waves, especially on the sea.

items.section: A · Adjectives and their opposites for describing textures
items.example: The ferry was delayed because of rough seas.
items.note: Rough seas suggests difficult, wavy water conditions; the plural is frequent.

items.pt: água calma; superfície da água lisa
items.section: A · Adjectives and their opposites for describing textures
items.example: The kayak glided across smooth water near the shore.
items.note: Smooth water has little wave movement; compare choppy water.

items.section: A · Adjectives and their opposites for describing textures
items.example: The wind turned the lake into choppy water by afternoon.
items.note: Choppy water is disturbed by small, irregular waves.

items.section: A · Adjectives and their opposites for describing textures
items.example: We practised paddling in calm water near the beach.
items.note: The answer key accepts calm as a natural contrast with rough lake water.

items.pt: estrada de piso regular; estrada sem irregularidades
items.section: A · Adjectives and their opposites for describing textures
items.example: The new motorway has a smooth road surface.
items.note: A smooth road offers an even ride, unlike a bumpy road.

items.section: A · Adjectives and their opposites for describing textures
items.example: The ambulance had to slow down on the bumpy road.
items.note: Bumpy describes a road whose uneven surface makes a vehicle shake.

items.section: A · Adjectives and their opposites for describing textures
items.example: We enjoyed a smooth flight despite the heavy rain.
items.note: Smooth flight means comfortable travel with little turbulence.

items.section: A · Adjectives and their opposites for describing textures
items.example: The storm made it a bumpy flight across the mountains.
items.note: Bumpy flight describes frequent jolts or turbulence, the opposite of smooth flight.

items.section: A · Adjectives and their opposites for describing textures
items.example: I sleep better with a soft pillow under my head.
items.note: Soft describes bedding that yields easily to pressure.

items.section: A · Adjectives and their opposites for describing textures
items.example: She prefers a firm pillow that supports her neck.
items.note: Firm conveys supportive resistance rather than extreme hardness; a natural contrast with soft pillow.

items.section: A · Adjectives and their opposites for describing textures
items.example: The hotel supplied a hard pillow that I found uncomfortable.
items.note: Hard can contrast with soft, but firm often sounds more positive for bedding.

items.section: A · Adjectives and their opposites for describing textures
items.example: The guest room has a soft bed with a thick mattress.
items.note: Soft describes a bed that compresses readily under weight.

items.section: A · Adjectives and their opposites for describing textures
items.example: My back feels more comfortable on a firm bed.
items.note: Firm suggests supportive resistance, as opposed to a very soft bed.

items.section: A · Adjectives and their opposites for describing textures
items.example: The heavy rain left soft ground around the garden.
items.note: Soft ground yields underfoot; hard ground does not.

items.section: A · Adjectives and their opposites for describing textures
items.example: The tent pegs were difficult to push into the hard ground.
items.note: Hard ground is firm and resistant to pressure.

items.section: A · Adjectives and their opposites for describing textures
items.example: Slow cooking can produce tender meat.
items.note: Tender meat is easy to chew; tough meat is its opposite.

items.pt: carne dura; carne difícil de mastigar
items.section: A · Adjectives and their opposites for describing textures
items.example: The steak was disappointing because it was tough meat.
items.note: Tough meat is hard to chew, not necessarily unpleasant in flavour.

items.section: A · Adjectives and their opposites for describing textures
items.example: The chef apologised for serving tough lamb chops.
items.note: An exercise-backed example of tough describing meat that is difficult to chew.

items.section: A · Adjectives and their opposites for describing textures
items.example: Use a sharp knife to slice the tomatoes neatly.
items.note: Sharp indicates a cutting edge that works well, contrasting with blunt knife.

items.section: A · Adjectives and their opposites for describing textures
items.example: A blunt knife crushed the bread instead of cutting it cleanly.
items.note: Blunt refers to a cutting edge that is no longer sharp.

items.pt: lápis apontado; lápis de ponta fina
items.section: A · Adjectives and their opposites for describing textures
items.example: A sharp pencil is useful for making precise marks.
items.note: A sharp pencil has a fine point; blunt pencil lacks a fine point.

items.pt: lápis sem ponta; lápis de ponta grossa
items.section: A · Adjectives and their opposites for describing textures
items.example: The drawing looked untidy because he used a blunt pencil.
items.note: A blunt pencil needs sharpening to regain a clear, narrow point.

items.section: A · Adjectives and their opposites for describing textures
items.example: He could barely cut the string with his blunt penknife.
items.note: Penknife is a small folding knife; blunt means its blade is not sharp.

items.section: B · Verbs relating to textures
items.example: Ice melts quickly on a hot metal tray.
items.note: Melt means change from solid ice to liquid water as temperature rises.

items.section: B · Verbs relating to textures
items.example: Snow melts slowly on the shaded side of the hill.
items.note: Melt is possible for snow as well as ice.

items.pt: a neve descongela; a neve começa a derreter
items.section: B · Verbs relating to textures
items.example: Snow thaws when the temperature stays above freezing.
items.note: Thaw describes frozen snow becoming unfrozen; melt is also possible with snow.

items.pt: a fruta amolece; a fruta fica mole
items.section: B · Verbs relating to textures
items.example: Fruit goes soft if it is kept for too long.
items.note: Go soft describes a gradual change in texture, often with ageing.

items.section: B · Verbs relating to textures
items.example: Bread goes hard if it is left uncovered overnight.
items.note: Go hard denotes bread losing its soft texture as it becomes stale.

items.pt: a voz se suaviza; o tom de voz fica mais gentil
items.section: B · Verbs relating to textures
items.example: A voice softens when someone begins to speak reassuringly.
items.note: Figurative soften describes a voice becoming gentler or more friendly.

items.pt: a voz endurece; o tom de voz fica mais severo
items.section: B · Verbs relating to textures
items.example: A voice hardens when frustration replaces patience.
items.note: Figurative harden describes a voice becoming sterner or less friendly.

items.pt: as atitudes ficam menos rígidas; as posições se suavizam
items.section: B · Verbs relating to textures
items.example: Attitudes soften when people begin listening to one another.
items.note: Soften can mean become less strict or hostile, not physically softer.

items.pt: as posições ficam mais rígidas; as atitudes se endurecem
items.section: B · Verbs relating to textures
items.example: Attitudes harden when negotiations repeatedly fail.
items.note: Harden can mean become more fixed, severe or less willing to compromise.

items.section: C · Other texture words with their collocations
items.example: The designer chose a matt finish to reduce reflections.
items.note: In British English, matt means not shiny; contrast a gloss finish.

items.section: C · Other texture words with their collocations
items.example: The cabinet doors have a gloss finish that reflects the ceiling lights.
items.note: Gloss describes a shiny finish; matt is its non-reflective opposite.

items.section: C · Other texture words with their collocations
items.example: Matt paint helps hide minor imperfections in the wall.
items.note: Matt paint dries with a non-shiny finish; British spelling is matt.

items.pt: tinta brilhante; tinta esmalte com brilho
items.section: C · Other texture words with their collocations
items.example: They used gloss paint on the wooden door.
items.note: Gloss paint produces a shiny surface and contrasts with matt paint.

items.section: C · Other texture words with their collocations
items.example: We ordered gloss photos for the family album.
items.note: Gloss describes the shiny finish on photographic prints.

items.pt: uma textura lisa; uma textura homogênea
items.section: C · Other texture words with their collocations
items.example: This yoghurt has a smooth texture without lumps.
items.note: Smooth texture describes an even consistency, often desirable in food or cosmetics.

items.section: C · Other texture words with their collocations
items.example: The sauce has a creamy texture without any added cream.
items.note: Creamy refers to a rich, soft and smooth consistency; not necessarily to an ingredient.

items.section: C · Other texture words with their collocations
items.example: Stir finely chopped cucumber into the yoghurt.
items.note: Finely chopped means cut into very small pieces, as opposed to coarsely chopped.

items.pt: legumes picados grosseiramente; legumes em pedaços grandes
items.section: C · Other texture words with their collocations
items.example: Add coarsely chopped vegetables to the pot.
items.note: Coarsely chopped describes relatively large pieces; the source explains it as the contrast to finely chopped.

items.section: C · Other texture words with their collocations
items.example: Sprinkle a little coarse sea salt over the roasted vegetables.
items.note: Coarse describes grains or particles that are relatively large; the lesson has coarse-grain sea salt.

items.section: C · Other texture words with their collocations
items.example: Fine grains of salt dissolve faster than large crystals.
items.note: Fine grains are small; contrast the coarse grains described in the unit.

items.section: C · Other texture words with their collocations
items.example: Add crushed garlic to the pan near the end of cooking.
items.note: Crushed is the usual adjective for garlic pressed or broken into small pieces.

items.section: C · Other texture words with their collocations
items.example: The conditioner left her with glossy hair.
items.note: Glossy means attractively shiny; do not confuse it with greasy, which is usually negative.

items.section: C · Other texture words with their collocations
items.example: He washed his greasy hands after repairing the bicycle.
items.note: Greasy describes hands covered with oil or fat, generally an unpleasant texture.

items.section: C · Other texture words with their collocations
items.example: The children had sticky fingers after eating the sweets.
items.note: Sticky means covered with a substance that tends to adhere to other surfaces.

items.section: D · Metaphorical uses of texture words
items.example: The presentation should go smoothly if we test the equipment first.
items.note: Go smoothly means happen without difficulty, not move along a physically smooth surface.

items.pt: ter a língua afiada; fazer comentários mordazes
items.section: D · Metaphorical uses of texture words
items.example: She can have a sharp tongue when she is annoyed.
items.note: A sharp tongue means a tendency to say cutting or unkind things.

items.pt: uma situação complicada; uma saia justa
items.section: D · Metaphorical uses of texture words
items.example: He found himself in a sticky situation after promising both teams the same room.
items.note: An informal expression for an awkward or difficult predicament; not literally sticky.

items.section: D · Metaphorical uses of texture words
items.example: The host asked the comedian to avoid coarse jokes.
items.note: Coarse figuratively describes crude or vulgar humour, rather than a rough physical texture.

items.section: D · Metaphorical uses of texture words
items.example: The moon rose against the velvety sky.
items.note: Velvety describes an unusually soft, deep or smooth visual quality, especially in dark scenes.
